entry: [[Spitz]]-type dog breed originally from northern [[China]]. A research study traced its origin to indigenous dogs in central China about 8,300 years ago. The breed has a sturdy, square-profiled build, a dense double coat, and a blue-black or purple tongue. The Chinese used Chows to pull dog sleds through swampy terrain, a practice noted by [[Marco Polo]]. The American Kennel Club registers approximately 10,000 Chow Chows a year.

French poet and trouvère (fl. c. 1160–1191). Chrétien wrote on [[King Arthur|Arthurian]] subjects, the Matter of Britain, in five major poems written in rhyming eight-syllable couplets. They include *Erec and Enide* (c. 1170), *Cligès* (c. 1176), *Yvain, the Knight of the Lion*, and *Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart*. *Yvain* is generally considered his most masterful work, and its structure has been seen as a step toward the [[Novel|modern novel]]. He completed only 9,000 lines of *Perceval, the Story of the Grail*, written between 1181 and 1190; four successors added 54,000 lines. Chrétien served Marie of France, Countess of Champagne, a daughter of King Louis VII and [[Eleanor of Aquitaine]]. Of his four poems based on [[Ovid]]'s *Metamorphoses*, only *Philomela* survives.

Canadian professional wrestler and two-time world champion. He held 30 championships in promotions including [[WWE]], World Championship Wrestling, and New Japan Pro-Wrestling, and he won the 2004 Royal Rumble. In 2007 he murdered his wife and seven-year-old son and then killed himself. Subsequent research suggested that depression and advanced [[Chronic traumatic encephalopathy]] were likely contributing factors. His legacy in [[Professional wrestling|professional wrestling]] remains controversial, although many regard his technical ability as exceptional.

American singer, songwriter, dancer, and actor. His debut single, "Run It!", topped the Billboard Hot 100 chart, and his album *F.A.M.E.* (2011) was his first to top the Billboard 200. He has sold over 140 million records worldwide. In 2009 he pleaded guilty to felony assault of his then-girlfriend, the singer [[Rihanna]], and received five years' probation. He has won 219 awards from 566 nominations.

American comedian and actor. Farley performed with Second City in [[Chicago]] before joining the cast of [[Saturday Night Live]] from 1990 to 1995. He was known for physical comedy and appeared in films including *Tommy Boy* and *Black Sheep*. He struggled with obesity, alcoholism, and substance abuse. He was found dead in his Chicago apartment from an accidental overdose of cocaine and morphine, with advanced heart disease also a factor. He received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] posthumously, in 2005.

American actor and producer. His films as a leading actor have grossed over $15.2 billion worldwide. Pratt played Andy Dwyer in the [[NBC]] sitcom *Parks and Recreation* and Star-Lord in six films of the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]]. He also starred as Owen Grady in *Jurassic World* and voiced roles in *The Lego Movie* franchise and *The Super Mario Bros. Movie*. He received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 2017. He has owned the production company Indivisible Productions since February 2020.

American comedian, actor, and filmmaker. Rock rose to prominence with [[Stand-up comedy|stand-up]] routines in the 1980s on race relations and human sexuality. He was a cast member of [[Saturday Night Live]] from 1990 to 1993 and later hosted the HBO talk show *The Chris Rock Show* (1997–2000). He has won three [[Grammy Awards]] for Best Comedy Album and four Primetime Emmy Awards. He hosted the [[Academy Awards]] in 2005 and 2016, and he was assaulted by [[Will Smith]] at the 2022 Awards.

[[Art Deco]] statue of [[Jesus]] in [[Rio de Janeiro]], [[Brazil]]. Designed by French-Polish sculptor Paul Landowski with Brazilian engineer Heitor da Silva Costa and French engineer Albert Caquot, it was built of reinforced concrete and clad in soapstone between 1922 and 1931. The face was sculpted by [[Romania|Romanian]] sculptor Gheorghe Leonida. The statue is 30 m high, excluding an 8 m pedestal, with arms 28 m wide, and weighs 635 metric tons. It stands on the peak of Corcovado mountain in Tijuca National Park. The original plan showed Christ holding a globe and a cross, but the design was changed to open arms. It is the largest Art Deco–style [[Sculpture|sculpture]] in the world and a symbol of [[Christianity]]. It was voted one of the New 7 Wonders of the World, and lightning damaged it in 2008.

Largest city in the [[South Island]] of [[New Zealand]]. It lies on the east coast of the Canterbury Region and had an urban population of 407,800 and a metropolitan population of 556,500. Its Māori name is Ōtautahi, and it is known as the Garden City for its English-style architecture and gardens. British settlement began in the mid-19th century, and the city received letters patent on July 31, 1856. Earthquakes from September 2010 included a February 22, 2011 quake that killed 185 people and led to a long rebuilding effort. It is one of five Antarctic gateway cities.

Two terrorist mass shootings at mosques in New Zealand on March 15, 2019. Brenton Tarrant, an Australian, attacked the Al Noor Mosque and the Linwood Islamic Centre during Friday prayer, killing 51 people and injuring 89 others. In 2020 he pleaded guilty to 51 murders, 40 attempted murders, and a terrorist act, and he received life imprisonment without parole. The attacks were mainly motivated by [[White supremacy|white supremacist]] beliefs and white nationalism. Prime Minister [[Jacinda Ardern]] called them a "well-planned" terrorist attack.

Dutch mathematician, physicist, astronomer, and inventor. Huygens made seminal contributions to optics and mechanics and is regarded as a key figure in the [[Scientific Revolution]]. He invented the [[Pendulum|pendulum]] clock, patented in 1657, which was the most accurate timekeeper for almost 300 years. In 1655 he discovered [[Titan (moon)|Titan]], Saturn's largest moon, and explained Saturn's appearance as a thin, flat ring. His wave theory of light, set out in *Traité de la Lumière* (1690), was initially rejected in favor of [[Isaac Newton]]'s corpuscular theory until [[Augustin-Jean Fresnel]] adapted Huygens's principle in 1821. In 1659 he derived the formula for [[Centrifugal force]] geometrically, a decade before Newton.

English actor known for physical transformations. His breakthrough came at age 13 in the 1987 war film *Empire of the Sun*, directed by [[Steven Spielberg]]. He gained wider recognition for *American Psycho* (2000) and *The Machinist* (2004). He played [[Batman]] in [[Christopher Nolan]]'s *The Dark Knight* trilogy. He won an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for *The Fighter* (2010), and a Golden Globe for portraying [[Dick Cheney]] in *Vice* (2018).

Christian democratic and conservative political party in Germany. Founded in 1945 as an interdenominational party, it is the major centre-right party in German politics and is generally pro-European. Germany's three longest-serving post-war chancellors, [[Konrad Adenauer]], [[Helmut Kohl]], and [[Angela Merkel]], all came from the party. It leads a grand coalition with the [[Social Democratic Party of Germany|SPD]], and Friedrich Merz has led the party since January 31, 2022. Its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union, runs in Bavaria instead. The CDU and CSU together won 28.5% of votes in the 2025 federal election.

Nontrinitarian Christian religion founded by [[Mary Baker Eddy]] in 1879 in New England. Adherents teach that sin, sickness, and death are illusions and that disease is healed through prayer rather than [[Medicine|medicine]]. The church does not forbid medical care but holds that prayer is most effective without it. Its newspaper, *The Christian Science Monitor*, won seven [[Pulitzer Prize|Pulitzer Prizes]] between 1950 and 2002. Membership reached nearly 270,000 by 1936 and was reported under 50,000 by 2009. Between the 1880s and 1990s several parents and others were prosecuted for manslaughter or neglect after relying on prayer.

Ideology inspired by Christian social teaching. It drew mainly on Catholic social teaching and neo-scholasticism and later gained ground among Lutherans and Pentecostals. In the 19th century its concerns included reconciling Catholicism with democracy and answering the "social question" of capitalism and the working class. In the 20th century Christian democrats led postwar Western and Southern Europe in building welfare states and constructing the [[European Union]]. Christian democrats support a social market economy. They are usually socially conservative and generally skeptical of [[Abortion]] and [[Same-sex marriage]]. Its position has been considered centre-left on economics and centre-right on social and moral issues. Major parties include the [[Christian Democratic Union of Germany]].

Distinct religious group within [[Christianity]], identifiable by name, history, organization, leadership, and doctrine. Divisions are defined by authority and doctrine, such as the nature of Jesus and papal primacy. Unlike a [[Cult|cult]] or [[Sect|sect]], a denomination is usually seen as part of the Christian mainstream. The [[Catholic Church]] has over 1.3 billion members, or 50.1% of Christians worldwide. The [[Eastern Orthodox Church]] has an estimated 220 million adherents, and the total [[Protestantism|Protestant]] population reached around 1.047 billion in 2024.

Philosophy developed by Christians or in direct relation to Christianity. It emerged to reconcile science, reason, and faith. [[Origen]] and [[Augustine of Hippo]] saw a harmonious relationship between faith and science, while [[Tertullian]] claimed contradiction. It developed in the Patristic period from about the 3rd century, and Scholasticism was its main form from the 11th century. The [[Catholic Church]] endorses no single official Catholic philosophy but holds that human reason can attain truths about God and morality. [[Thomas Aquinas]] is often cited as an exemplar of synthesizing philosophy and theology. Some scholars question whether a distinct Christian philosophy exists, arguing that its ideas are inherited from Greek thought.

British-Iranian journalist and television host. Amanpour is chief international anchor for [[CNN]] and hosts *Amanpour & Company* on [[PBS]]. She joined CNN in 1983 and gained wide notice for reporting from the [[Gulf War]] and the [[Bosnian War]]. Viewers and critics questioned her objectivity, arguing that some of her reports from the [[Siege of Sarajevo]] favored the Bosnian Muslims. She replied that objectivity means giving each side a hearing.

Adherents of [[Christianity]], a monotheistic religion based on the life and teachings of [[Jesus]]. A 2011 Pew Research Center survey counted 2.3 billion Christians worldwide, about 37% living in the [[Americas]] and 26% in [[Europe]]. Christians form the majority in 158 countries and territories. About half are Catholic, and more than a third (37%) are Protestant. The term first appears in the New Testament, in Acts 11, at [[Antioch]].

American model and actress. Brinkley appeared on three consecutive *Sports Illustrated* Swimsuit Issue covers from 1979 to 1981, a first. She was the face of CoverGirl for 25 years and has appeared on over 500 magazine covers. She was married to musician [[Billy Joel]] from 1985 to 1994. She has also worked as an illustrator, photographer, writer, and designer, and she is an activist for human and [[Animal rights|animal rights]] and the environment.

American singer and songwriter. Her self-titled debut album (1999) topped the US Billboard 200 and garnered three US Billboard Hot 100 number-one singles. She has sold over 100 million records worldwide and has won five [[Grammy Awards]] and two Latin Grammy Awards. She has a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]]. [[Time (magazine)|Time]] named her one of the 100 most influential people in the world in 2013.

Queen of Sweden (r. 1632–1654), of the House of Vasa. She succeeded her father, Gustavus Adolphus, at the age of five after his death at the Battle of Lützen, and she began ruling at 18. She was among the most erudite women of the 17th century and wanted Stockholm to become the "Athens of the North". Her lavish spending pushed the state towards bankruptcy, and she argued for peace to end the [[Thirty Years' War]]. Her conversion to Catholicism and refusal to marry led her to abdicate in 1654 and settle in [[Rome]]. She protected many [[Baroque]] artists and composers, and she is one of the few women buried in the Vatican Grottoes.

French lawyer and politician, president of the European Central Bank since 2019. She was managing director of the [[International Monetary Fund]] from 2011 to 2019 and was the first woman to hold that post and the post of French minister of economy, finance, and industry. As minister from 2007 to 2011, she oversaw the government response to the [[2008 financial crisis]]. In December 2016 a French court convicted her of negligence over the Bernard Tapie arbitration but imposed no penalty.

Venetian-born French court writer and poet. Her father, a physician and astrologer, was invited to the French court in 1368 and insisted that she learn Latin, philosophy, and science, unusual for a girl of her era. After her husband died of the plague in 1389, she supported her children and mother by writing for patrons including Louis I of Orléans and Philip the Bold of Burgundy. She has been called the first professional woman of letters in Europe. Her best-known works, *The Book of the City of Ladies* and *The Treasure of the City of Ladies*, are considered among the earliest feminist writings. She also wrote a poem celebrating the victories of [[Joan of Arc]].

Christian holiday commemorating the birth of [[Jesus|Jesus Christ]], observed chiefly on December 25. Preparation begins on the First Sunday of Advent, and in the West Christmastide historically lasted twelve days. The New Testament Nativity narrative says Jesus was born in [[Bethlehem]]. In the early 4th century the church fixed the date as December 25, the date of the [[Winter solstice|winter solstice]] in the Roman Empire. Most Christians celebrate in the [[Gregorian calendar]], while parts of the Eastern churches use the [[Julian calendar]], which corresponds to January 7. Customs include gift-giving and Christmas trees, and figures such as [[Santa Claus]] and [[Saint Nicholas]] bring gifts to children. The English name is a shortened form of "Christ's Mass".
